claim: The study provides transcriptome-wide RNA-binding profiles of 30 general RNA degradation factors in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Here we provide transcriptome-wide RNA-binding profiles of 30 general RNA degradation factors in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including Figure 1B showing the number of cross-link sites obtained for each factor.

claim: The profiles reveal the distribution of degradation factors between different RNA classes.
source: The profiles reveal the distribution of degradation factors between different RNA classes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2, which shows the fractions of PAR-CLIP reads falling into various transcript classes and enrichment scores for different RNA classes.

claim: The profiles are consistent with the canonical degradation pathway for closed-loop forming mRNAs after deadenylation.
source: They are consistent with the canonical degradation pathway for closed-loop forming mRNAs after deadenylation.
evidence: This is supported by the metagene profiles in Figure 3 showing deadenylation factors binding near the pA site and decapping factors binding near the 3' end, consistent with closed-loop formation.

claim: Most degradation factors bind intact mRNAs based on modeling with mRNA half-lives.
source: Modeling based on mRNA half-lives suggests that most degradation factors bind intact mRNAs, whereas decapping factors are recruited only for mRNA degradation, consistent with decapping being a rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling analysis in Figure 7B, which shows the relationship between factor occupancy and mRNA half-life, with different a/b ratios for different factors.

claim: Decapping factors are recruited only for mRNA degradation.
source: Modeling based on mRNA half-lives suggests that most degradation factors bind intact mRNAs, whereas decapping factors are recruited only for mRNA degradation, consistent with decapping being a rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7B showing that Dcp2 has a very high a/b ratio (18.7), indicating preferential cross-linking to transcripts being degraded rather than intact mRNAs.

claim: Decapping is a rate-limiting step in mRNA degradation.
source: Modeling based on mRNA half-lives suggests that most degradation factors bind intact mRNAs, whereas decapping factors are recruited only for mRNA degradation, consistent with decapping being a rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that decapping factors, particularly Dcp2, are enriched on transcripts being degraded (high a/b ratio in Figure 7B), suggesting they are recruited specifically during degradation.

claim: Decapping factors preferentially bind mRNAs with non-optimal codons.
source: Decapping factors preferentially bind mRNAs with non-optimal codons, consistent with rapid degradation of inefficiently translated mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6A showing that decapping factors (Dcp2, Dhh1) have higher occupancy on transcripts with lower codon optimality, and Figure 6B showing Dcp2 enrichment on non-optimal codons.

claim: mRNAs with non-optimal codons are rapidly degraded.
source: Decapping factors preferentially bind mRNAs with non-optimal codons, consistent with rapid degradation of inefficiently translated mRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the preferential binding of decapping factors to non-optimal transcripts (Figure 6A, 6B) and the known function of decapping in initiating mRNA degradation.

claim: The nuclear surveillance machinery, including the complexes Nrd1/Nab3 and TRAMP4, targets aberrant nuclear RNAs.
source: Global analysis suggests that the nuclear surveillance machinery, including the complexes Nrd1/Nab3 and TRAMP4, targets aberrant nuclear RNAs and processes snoRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4 showing similar binding patterns of TRAMP4 subunits and exosome subunits to antisense RNAs as Nrd1/Nab3, and Figure 2 showing enrichment on CUTs and NUTs.

claim: The nuclear surveillance machinery processes snoRNAs.
source: Global analysis suggests that the nuclear surveillance machinery, including the complexes Nrd1/Nab3 and TRAMP4, targets aberrant nuclear RNAs and processes snoRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing TRAMP complex binding patterns around snoRNA genes, with TRAMP5 binding to gene bodies and TRAMP4 binding downstream of the 3' end.

claim: PAR-CLIP experiments for 30 degradation factors showed high reproducibility with Spearman correlations between 0.87 and 1.00 (mean: 0.94) between biological replicates.
source: The high reproducibility of these PAR-CLIP experiments is revealed by a comparison of two independent biological replicates that we collected for all 30 degradation factors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with Spearman correlations between 0.87 and 1.00 (mean: 0.94).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing scatter plots of replicate comparisons.

claim: Tens of thousands of verified factor-RNA cross-link sites with p-values≤0.005 were obtained for each factor.
source: We typically obtained tens of thousands of verified factor-RNA cross-link sites with p-values≤0.005 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, which displays the number of high-confidence cross-link sites for each factor.

claim: Most PAR-CLIP sequencing reads fall into the mRNA transcript class.
source: A first analysis revealed that most PAR-CLIP sequencing reads fall into the mRNA transcript class, although many of the factors also show a considerable number of sequencing reads in ncRNAs, in particular rRNAs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A, which displays the fractions of reads in different transcript classes.

claim: Many degradation factors show considerable numbers of sequencing reads in ncRNAs, particularly rRNAs.
source: A first analysis revealed that most PAR-CLIP sequencing reads fall into the mRNA transcript class, although many of the factors also show a considerable number of sequencing reads in ncRNAs, in particular rRNAs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The catalytic subunit Pop2 and core subunits Not1 and Caf40 of the Ccr4/Not complex have similar binding preferences for 5' UTR, CDS, 3' UTR of mRNAs, rRNAs, tRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs.
source: The catalytic subunit Pop2 and the core subunits Not1 and Caf40 of the deadenylase complex Ccr4/Not have similar binding preferences for the 5´ UTR, the CDS and 3´ UTR of mRNAs, for rRNAs, tRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs (Figure 2B, highlighted in red).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B with enrichment scores.

claim: Ccr4 has different binding preferences compared to other Ccr4/Not complex subunits and is strongly enriched at mRNA introns.
source: Compared to other deadenylation factors of the Ccr4/Not complex, the catalytically active subunit Ccr4 has different binding preferences, and is strongly enriched at mRNA introns.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2B showing distinct enrichment patterns for Ccr4.

claim: The Pan2/Pan3 deadenylation complex shows similar binding preferences as the Ccr4/Not complex (except for Ccr4).
source: The second deadenylation complex, Pan2/Pan3, shows a similar binding preference as the Ccr4/Not complex (except for the Ccr4 subunit), consistent with its dominant role in yeast mRNA deadenylation (Boeck et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the functional role, and can be observed in Figure 2B.

claim: Pan2/Pan3 has a dominant role in yeast mRNA deadenylation.
source: The second deadenylation complex, Pan2/Pan3, shows a similar binding preference as the Ccr4/Not complex (except for the Ccr4 subunit), consistent with its dominant role in yeast mRNA deadenylation (Boeck et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Boeck et al., 1996.

claim: Pan3 shows strong binding preference for rRNAs and tRNAs.
source: Pan3 shows a strong binding preference for rRNAs and tRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2B.

claim: All decapping-related factors show similar binding preferences among each other.
source: For all decapping-related factors we observed similar binding preferences among each other (Figure 2B, highlighted in green).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Decapping factors show strongest enrichment at SUTs and mRNAs compared to other transcript classes.
source: They show the strongest enrichment at SUTs and at mRNAs compared to the other transcript classes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2B.

claim: Decapping factors bind preferentially to CDS and 3' UTR as well as SUTs.
source: Decapping factors bind preferentially to CDS and 3´ UTR as well as SUTs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SUTs are degraded via Dcp2-dependent pathways in the cytoplasm.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that SUTs are degraded via Dcp2-dependent pathways in the cytoplasm (Marquardt et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2014; Thompson and Parker, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Dcp2 and Edc3 additionally bind to NUTs.
source: Dcp2, which harbors the hydrolase activity that removes the 5´ cap, and the decapping activator Edc3, additionally bind to NUTs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2B.

claim: Xrn1 shows similar binding preference as decapping factors.
source: The 5´ exonuclease Xrn1 shows a similar binding preference as the decapping factors (Figure 2B, highlighted in orange).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Exosome core subunits Csl4 and Rrp40 show similar cross-linking to rRNAs, tRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs.
source: The core exosome subunits Csl4 and Rrp40 show similar cross-linking to rRNAs, tRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2B.

claim: The catalytic exosome subunit Rrp44 and core subunit Rrp4 bind to introns of mRNAs and preferentially to CUTs and NUTs.
source: The catalytic exosome subunit Rrp44 and the core subunit Rrp4 binds to introns of mRNAs, but preferentially to the short-lived, nuclear CUTs and NUTs.

claim: Rrp6 shows binding to rRNAs, snoRNAs, snRNAs, CUTs and NUTs.

evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rrp6 is needed for nuclear processing of non-coding transcripts and degradation of short-lived nuclear transcripts.
source: This is consistent with the suggestion that the factor is needed for nuclear processing of such non-coding transcripts and degradation of short-lived nuclear transcripts (Heo et al., 2013; Vasiljeva and Buratowski, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies (Heo et al., 2013; Vasiljeva and Buratowski, 2006).

claim: TRAMP4 and TRAMP5 complexes show clearly distinct cross-linking patterns.
source: The two TRAMP complexes TRAMP4 and TRAMP5 show clearly distinct cross-linking patterns (Figure 2B, highlighted in light blue).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TRAMP4 subunits (Mtr4, Air2, Trf4) are enriched in introns, SUTs, CUTs, and NUTs.
source: TRAMP4 subunits (Mtr4, Air2, Trf4) are enriched in introns, consistent with a function on mRNAs, and on SUTs, CUTs, and NUTs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TRAMP5 complex (Mtr4, Air1, Trf5) shows binding enrichment for introns, rRNAs, tRNAs, snRNAs, and snoRNAs.
source: The TRAMP5 complex (Mtr4, Air1, Trf5) shows binding enrichment for introns, rRNAs, tRNAs, snRNAs, and snoRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TRAMP5 binding to rRNAs is in agreement with previous data showing rRNA binding for Mtr4 and exosome subunits.
source: This is in agreement with previous data, which showed rRNA binding for Mtr4 and exosome subunits (Delan-Forino et al., 2017; Schneider and Tollervey, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies (Delan-Forino et al., 2017; Schneider and Tollervey, 2013).

claim: The TRAMP complex cooperates with the Nrd1/Nab3 complex and nuclear exosome during maturation and 3' pre-processing of snoRNAs.
source: Moreover, the TRAMP complex cooperates with the Nrd1/Nab3 complex and the nuclear exosome complex during the maturation and 3´ pre-processing of snoRNAs (Grzechnik and Kufel, 2008).

claim: Air2/Trf4 bind downstream of the 3' end of snoRNA genes.

claim: TRAMP4 may work together with the Nrd1/Nab3 machinery to pre-process snoRNAs.
source: This suggests that TRAMP5 is mainly involved in snoRNA degradation, whereas TRAMP4 may work together with the Nrd1/Nab3 machinery to pre-process snoRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and to target NUTs, SUTs, and CUTs for degradation (Figure 2B, highlighted in light blue).
evidence: This is inferred from the binding patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2B.

claim: All Ski complex subunits bind the 5' UTR, CDS, and 3' UTR of mRNAs, rRNAs, tRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs.
source: All Ski complex subunits bind the 5´ UTR, CDS, and 3´ UTR of mRNAs, rRNAs, tRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ski2 preferentially binds to the CDS of mRNAs.
source: The Ski2 subunit preferentially binds to the CDS of mRNAs, consistent with its function as a helicase to detach bound proteins from the mRNAs (Houseley and Tollervey, 2009; Lebreton and Séraphin, 2008).

claim: Ski7 preferentially binds rRNAs and tRNAs.
source: The exosome adaptor subunit Ski7 preferentially binds rRNAs and tRNAs.

source: Finally, we observed similar cross-linking patterns for all NMD factors with strong binding to SUTs and NUTs (Figure 2B, highlighted in yellow).

source: Upf3 also binds to the 5´ UTR, CDS, and 3´ UTR of mRNAs, and Nmd4 binds to introns and 3´ UTRs of mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nmd4 binds to introns and 3' UTRs of mRNAs.
source: Upf3 also binds to the 5´ UTR, CDS, and 3´ UTR of mRNAs, and Nmd4 binds to introns and 3´ UTRs of mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pan2/Pan3 deadenylase complex and Ccr4/Not subunits Pop2, Not1, and Caf40 cross-link upstream of the 3' end of mRNA with highest enrichment at the pA site.
source: The Pan2/Pan3 deadenylase complex and the Ccr4/Not subunits Pop2, Not1, and Caf40 all cross-link upstream of the 3´ end of mRNA with the highest enrichment at the pA site, as expected from their function in shortening the polyA tail.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ccr4 binds strongly in the 5' region of mRNAs.
source: The catalytic subunit Ccr4 binds strongly in the 5´ region of mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: All 5' decapping factors bind upstream of the pA site.
source: All 5´ decapping factors bind upstream of the pA site, and all but the catalytically active subunit Dcp2 show increasing occupancy towards the 3´ end of mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: All decapping factors except Dcp2 show increasing occupancy towards the 3' end of mRNAs.
source: All 5´ decapping factors bind upstream of the pA site, and all but the catalytically active subunit Dcp2 show increasing occupancy towards the 3´ end of mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dcp2 binds almost exclusively at the pA site.
source: In contrast, Dcp2 binds almost exclusively at the pA site, suggesting that it might be recruited only upon active mRNA degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dcp2 might be recruited only upon active mRNA degradation.
source: In contrast, Dcp2 binds almost exclusively at the pA site, suggesting that it might be recruited only upon active mRNA degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding pattern of Dcp2 shown in Figure 3 and further supported by the modeling analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: Xrn1 has highest occupancy towards the 3' end of mRNAs.
source: The cytoplasmic 5´ exonuclease Xrn1 has the highest occupancy towards the 3´ end, similar to the previously published crosslinking and cDNA analysis (CRAC) data (Tuck and Tollervey, 2013), thereby resembling the binding profiles of the decapping factors.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to previous CRAC data, and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Xrn1 binding profile resembles that of decapping factors.
source: The cytoplasmic 5´ exonuclease Xrn1 has the highest occupancy towards the 3´ end, similar to the previously published crosslinking and cDNA analysis (CRAC) data (Tuck and Tollervey, 2013), thereby resembling the binding profiles of the decapping factors.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed by comparing Xrn1 and decapping factor profiles in Figure 3.

claim: The binding preference of degradation factors lies at the end of the 3' UTR independent of the stop codon position.
source: Comparison of the binding profiles aligned at the pA site or alternatively with profiles aligned at the translation stop codon shows that the binding preference indeed lies at the end of the 3´ UTR independent of the stop codon position (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Exosome core subunits (Csl4, Rrp40, Rrp4) and catalytically active subunits (Rrp6, Rrp44) cross-link to the 5' end of transcripts.
source: The exosome core subunits (Csl4, Rrp40, and Rrp4) and the catalytically active subunits (nuclear: Rrp6, cytoplasmic: Rrp44) cross-link to the 5´ end of the transcript (Figure 3), possibly because the exosome binds to the 5´ end while digesting the 3´ end, or more likely because the exosome slows down towards the remaining 5´ end of mRNAs after rapid degradation from the 3´ end.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both TRAMP complexes bind mainly in the 5' region of mRNAs near the TSS.
source: Both TRAMP complexes bind mainly in the 5´ region of mRNAs near the TSS, as previously observed for Mtr4 and Trf4 (Tuck and Tollervey, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to previous work, and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ski7 and Ski8 occupy the entire mRNA with increasing occupancy towards the pA site.
source: The Ski complex components Ski7 and Ski8 occupy the entire mRNA with increasing occupancy towards the pA site, whereas Ski2 and Ski3 show more discrete binding towards the polyA tail (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ski2 and Ski3 show discrete binding towards the polyA tail.
source: The Ski complex components Ski7 and Ski8 occupy the entire mRNA with increasing occupancy towards the pA site, whereas Ski2 and Ski3 show more discrete binding towards the polyA tail (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: NMD factors Upf1 and Upf3 show binding over the entire mRNA with highest occupancy at the pA site.
source: The NMD factors Upf1 and Upf3 show binding over the entire mRNA with highest occupancy at the pA site, consistent with their role in scanning for premature stop codons in mRNAs and remodeling of the 3´ end of protein-RNA complexes and completion of mRNA decay (Franks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation supporting the functional interpretation, and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Upf2 and Nmd4 show strongest binding near the 3' ends of mRNAs.
source: In addition, Upf2 and Nmd4 show strongest binding near the 3´ ends of mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: All exosome subunits (Rrp6, Csl4, Rrp40, Rrp4, Rrp44) and TRAMP4 complex subunits (Mtr4, Air2, Trf4) show similar binding patterns to Nrd1 and Nab3 for upstream antisense RNA.
source: Indeed, we observed a similar binding pattern for all exosome subunits (Rrp6, Csl4, Rrp40, Rrp4, Rrp44) and subunits of the TRAMP4 complex (Mtr4, Air2, Trf4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Exosome subunits and TRAMP4 factors show strong enrichment of Nrd1 and Nab3 motifs (GTAG, CTTG) around their cross-link sites.
source: Consistent with this, these factors also bind strongly to previously annotated NUTs and CUTs (Figure 2) and show strong enrichment of Nrd1 and Nab3 motifs (GTAG, CTTG) around their cross-link sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRAMP4 and exosome subunits show strong preference for binding to the upstream promoter region of genes controlled by the Nrd1/Nab3 complex.
source: TRAMP4 and the exosome subunits show a strong preference for binding to the upstream promoter region of genes that are controlled by the Nrd1/Nab3 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The upstream signal for Air2 and Mtr4 originates primarily from NUTs and CUTs.
source: To further confirm that this upstream signal originates from NUTs and CUTs, we excluded cross-link sites that fall within such previously annotated regions. We then compared the binding profiles generated from the remaining binding sites on mRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Upon filtering, the signal upstream of the TSS for Air2 and Mtr4 decreases, showing that Nrd1-mediated regulation is the primary cause for this upstream signal.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by comparing Figure 3 with Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Most of the antisense signal originates from transcripts targeted by the Nrd1/Nab3 machinery.
source: Comparison of the observed antisense profiles (Figure 4) with those obtained after excluding cross-link sites in previously annotated NUT and CUT regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) confirms that most of the signal originates from transcripts that are targeted by the Nrd1/Nab3 machinery.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by comparing Figure 4 with Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: TRAMP4 can add a short polyA tail on aberrant RNAs.
source: Indeed, it was reported that TRAMP4 can add a short polyA tail on aberrant RNAs (Wyers et al., 2005), which may trigger degradation by the nuclear exosome.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wyers et al., 2005.

claim: Short polyA tails added by TRAMP4 may trigger degradation by the nuclear exosome.
source: Indeed, it was reported that TRAMP4 can add a short polyA tail on aberrant RNAs (Wyers et al., 2005), which may trigger degradation by the nuclear exosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of TRAMP4 and the observed binding patterns.

claim: Nrd1 and Trf4 interact.
source: It was also recently shown that Nrd1 and Trf4 interact, providing a basis for coupling surveillance-mediated termination to RNA degradation (Tudek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tudek et al., 2014.

claim: The analysis recovers several established interactions between subunits of known complexes and between different complexes.
source: This extensive global analysis suggests which factors reside in functional complexes and which functional complexes may interact during RNA processing and degradation. The analysis recovers several established interactions between subunits of known complexes and between different complexes, providing a positive control.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by the co-occupancy and co-localization analyses in Figure 5.

claim: All factors of the decapping complex show very high co-occupancy and co-localization.
source: For example, all factors of the decapping complex show very high co-occupancy and co-localization, as do Air2 and Mtr4, which reside in the TRAMP4 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Air2 and Mtr4 show very high co-occupancy and co-localization.
source: For example, all factors of the decapping complex show very high co-occupancy and co-localization, as do Air2 and Mtr4, which reside in the TRAMP4 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Ccr4 has a role in transcription elongation.
source: The degradation factors Ccr4 and Air1 also reside in this cluster, maybe reflecting the role of Ccr4 in transcription elongation (Kruk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Kruk et al., 2011.

claim: Rai1 detects and removes incomplete 5' cap structures to subject aberrant pre-mRNAs to nuclear degradation.
source: Rai1 has been shown to detect and remove incomplete 5´ cap structures, to subject aberrant pre-mRNAs to nuclear degradation (Jiao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Jiao et al., 2010.

claim: The high correlation between Xrn1 and Ski2 has been reported in a CRAC experiment.
source: The high correlation between Xrn1 and Ski2 has been reported in a CRAC experiment (Tuck and Tollervey, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tuck and Tollervey, 2013.

claim: The 5' decapping machinery and Xrn1 preferentially bind transcripts with low transcript optimality.
source: We found that the 5´ decapping machinery and Xrn1 preferentially bind transcripts with low transcript optimality.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The 3' deadenylation machinery and the exosome bind more strongly to optimal transcripts.
source: In contrast, the 3´ deadenylation machinery and the exosome bind more strongly to optimal transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Dcp2 enrichment score is high on non-optimal codons and low on optimal codons.
source: For Dcp2 this enrichment score is high on non-optimal codons, and low on optimal codons, whereas the opposite trend is observed for Ccr4 and most degradation factors (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1–7)

claim: Ccr4 shows the opposite codon enrichment trend compared to Dcp2, with enrichment on optimal codons.
source: For Dcp2 this enrichment score is high on non-optimal codons, and low on optimal codons, whereas the opposite trend is observed for Ccr4 and most degradation factors (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1–7)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ribosome stalling on translationally inefficient codons can lead to recruitment of Dcp2 and Xrn1 and subsequent 5' degradation of the transcript.
source: This is consistent with a model that ribosome stalling on translationally inefficient codons can lead to recruitment of Dcp2 and Xrn1 and subsequent 5´ degradation of the transcript (Heck and Wilusz, 2018).

evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C using multivariate linear regression analysis.

claim: NMD factors Upf1 and Upf3 bind non-optimal transcripts.

source: On both stable and unstable mRNAs, Dcp1, Edc2, Edc3, and Dhh1 show increased binding near the 3´ end, but unstable RNAs show a higher occupancy in the transcript body.

claim: Unstable RNAs show higher occupancy of decapping factors in the transcript body compared to stable RNAs.
source: On both stable and unstable mRNAs, Dcp1, Edc2, Edc3, and Dhh1 show increased binding near the 3´ end, but unstable RNAs show a higher occupancy in the transcript body.

claim: Dcp2 binds almost exclusively at the 3' end and has higher occupancy on unstable transcripts.
source: The catalytically active subunit Dcp2 binds almost exclusively at the 3´ end and has a higher occupancy on unstable transcripts.

claim: Dcp2 has a binding preference for A-rich RNA sequences.

claim: Dcp2 shows a very high a/b ratio, revealing that it cross-links preferentially to transcripts that are being degraded.
source: In particular, Dcp2 shows a very high a/b ratio, revealing that it cross-links preferentially to transcripts that are being degraded.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B with an a/b ratio of 18.7 for Dcp2.

claim: The 5' decapping machinery, although present to some extent on complete mRNAs, is enriched when mRNAs are degraded.
source: This analysis strongly suggests that the 5´ decapping machinery, although present to some extent on complete mRNAs, is enriched when mRNAs are degraded.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the modeling analysis in Figure 7B showing different a/b ratios for decapping factors.

claim: The preferred localization of 5' decapping and 3' deadenylation factors near the mRNA 3' and 5' end, respectively, may be explained by formation of an mRNA closed-loop structure.
source: The preferred localization of 5´ decapping and 3´ deadenylation factors near the mRNA 3´ and 5´ end, respectively, seems counterintuitive, but may be explained by formation of an mRNA closed-loop structure by messenger ribonucleoproteins (mRNPs), where 5´ and 3´ ends are in proximity (Gallie, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Gallie, 1991.

claim: Mature mRNPs may carry decapping factors near their 3' end.
source: It is possible that mature mRNPs carry decapping factors near their 3´ end, and that upon polyA tail shorting the decapping complex is activated, leading to decapping and rapid RNA degradation from the 5´ end.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the observed binding patterns.

claim: Upon polyA tail shortening, the decapping complex may be activated, leading to decapping and rapid RNA degradation from the 5' end.
source: It is possible that mature mRNPs carry decapping factors near their 3´ end, and that upon polyA tail shorting the decapping complex is activated, leading to decapping and rapid RNA degradation from the 5´ end.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the observed binding patterns.

claim: Decapping would open the RNA closed-loop structure, providing access for exonucleases and allowing for rapid RNA removal.
source: In this model, decapping would open the RNA closed-loop structure, providing access for exonucleases and allowing for rapid RNA removal.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on the observed data.

claim: Decapping factors are enriched on translationally non-optimal codons, which agrees with previous findings suggesting a link between translation and RNA degradation from the 5' end through the decapping enhancer Dhh1.
source: Further, our result that decapping factors are enriched on translationally non-optimal codons agrees with previous findings that suggest a link between translation and RNA degradation from the 5´ end through the decapping enhancer Dhh1 (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: The Nrd1/Nab3 complex recognizes aberrant, antisense RNAs.
source: First, the Nrd1/Nab3 complex recognizes aberrant, antisense RNAs (Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Schulz et al., 2013.

claim: Aberrant RNAs recognized by Nrd1/Nab3 get adenylated by the TRAMP4 complex.
source: These RNAs then get adenylated by the TRAMP4 complex, consistent with an interaction of the Nrd1/Nab3 complex and the TRAMP subunit Trf4 (Tudek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tudek et al., 2014.

claim: The short polyA tail added by TRAMP4 targets the RNA for degradation by the nuclear exosome.
source: The short polyA tail targets the RNA for degradation by the nuclear exosome.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for nuclear surveillance based on the observed binding patterns and known functions.

claim: Degradation of introns and ncRNAs upstream of mRNAs on the same strand (annotated as NUTs and CUTs) likely uses the same degradation mechanism as aberrant antisense RNAs.
source: We note that the degradation of introns and ncRNAs upstream of mRNAs on the same strand, which were annotated as NUTs and CUTs, is likely to use the same degradation mechanism because these are bound by the same factors (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar binding patterns observed for these RNA classes.

claim: Degradation of short-lived ncRNAs in the nucleus involves Nrd1/Nab3, TRAMP4, and the exosome.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with the idea that degradation of short-lived ncRNAs in the nucleus involves Nrd1/Nab3, TRAMP4, and the exosome.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observed binding patterns.

claim: The exosome is involved in 3'→5' cytoplasmic mRNA degradation and in the processing and degradation of long-lived transcripts such as tRNAs, rRNAs and sn(o)RNAs.
source: The exosome is involved in 3´→5´ cytoplasmic mRNA degradation, and in the processing and degradation of long-lived transcripts such as tRNAs, rRNAs and sn(o)RNAs.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and the observed binding patterns.

claim: Differences in exosome co-factor binding to different RNA classes support the hypothesis that these factors confer specificity for processing and degradation of various RNA species.
source: The differences in exosome co-factor binding to different RNA classes (Figure 2) support the hypothesis that these factors confer specificity for processing and degradation of various RNA species (Delan-Forino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Delan-Forino et al., 2017.

claim: Ski2 is important for initial RNA degradation by using its helicase activity to dissolve secondary structures and allowing the exosome to start degradation.
source: The exosome co-factor Ski2 shows cross-linking towards the 3´ end of mRNAs (Figure 3). This indicates that the subunit is important for initial RNA degradation by using its helicase activity to dissolve secondary structures and allowing the exosome to start degradation of the transcript (Schneider and Tollervey, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Schneider and Tollervey, 2013.

claim: Some mRNAs may be targeted by TRAMP5 for exosomal degradation.
source: Like the exosome complex, the exosome co-factor TRAMP5 binds mRNAs towards the 5´ end of transcripts, and thus some mRNAs may be targeted by TRAMP5 for exosomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed binding patterns.

claim: The exosome moves rapidly from 3'→5' and then slows down, causing extensive cross-linking near the mRNA 5' end.
source: The catalytic exosome subunits Rrp44 and Rrp6 and the exosome core cross-link near the mRNA 5´ end, probably because the exosome moves rapidly from 3´→5´ and then slows down, causing extensive cross-linking.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed binding patterns.

claim: PAR-CLIP was performed using a published protocol with minor modifications.
source: We performed PAR-CLIP in S. cerevisiae using our published protocol (Battaglia et al., 2017), with minor modifications (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the published protocol.

claim: Yeast cells were labeled with 1 mM 4-thiouracil for 4 hours.
source: Briefly, TAP-tagged protein expressing yeast cells were grown in minimal medium (CSM mixture, Formedium, UK) supplemented with 89 µM uracil, 50–100 µM 4-thiouracil (4tU) and 2% glucose at 30°C to OD600 = 0.5. Cells were labeled in 1 mM 4tU final concentration for 4 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Cells were UV irradiated with 10–12 J/cm2 at a wavelength of 365 nm.
source: After labeling, cells were harvested, resuspended in ice-cold PBS and UV irradiated with 10–12 J/cm2 at a wavelength of 365 nm on ice and continuous shaking.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Immunoprecipitation was performed with rabbit IgG-conjugated Protein G magnetic beads.
source: The cleared lysate was used for immunoprecipitation with rabbit IgG-conjugated Protein G magnetic beads (Invitrogen, Germany) on a rotating wheel for 4 hr or overnight at 4°C.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Partial digest of cross-linked RNA was performed with 50 U RNase T1 per mL for 15–25 min at 25°C.
source: Partial digest of the cross-linked RNA was performed with 50 U RNase T1 per mL for 15–25 min at 25°C.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 50–75 nt single-end sequencing was performed on Illumina sequencers (HiSeq1500, HiSeq2500 and NextSeq550).
source: Quantification on an Agilent 2200 TapeStation instrument (Agilent Technologies, Germany) and 50–75 nt single-end sequencing was performed on Illumina sequencers (HiSeq1500, HiSeq2500 and NextSeq550).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mapping and statistical evaluation of PAR-CLIP experiments was performed using the in-house software mockinbird.
source: Mapping and statistical evaluation of PAR-CLIP experiments was performed using our in-house software mockinbird (Roth and Torkler, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: A stringent cutoff of 0.005 for the p-value of cross-link sites was used to obtain high confidence cross-link sites.
source: To obtain high confidence cross-link sites, we set a stringent cutoff of 0.005 for the p-value of cross-link sites and require a minimum coverage of 2 per site.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A minimum coverage of 2 per site was required for high confidence cross-link sites.
source: To obtain high confidence cross-link sites, we set a stringent cutoff of 0.005 for the p-value of cross-link sites and require a minimum coverage of 2 per site.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Occupancy of a factor on a verified cross-link site is defined as the number of transitions divided by the concentration of RNAs covering the cross-link site according to the input library control.
source: Finally, the occupancy of a factor on a verified cross-link site is defined as the number of transitions obtained from our PAR-CLIP experiments divided by the concentration of RNAs covering the cross-link site according to the input library control.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
